We don't take vacations. 15 days is the average amount of vacation we take, and that's down from 21 days in the year 2000. 169 million days of unused vacation a year valued at over $52 billion. This idea that we go from high school to college, to career, perhaps have a family, at the end, we accumulate some wealth, and that is how we get respect. This idea that making money and having things is much more valued and celebrated than having enriching experiences. Who here knows what a gap year is? Who's been on a gap year? Keep your hand raised. I've seen some hands. Well, very simply, a gap year is taking six months or a year off, after high school or maybe after college, before starting your career, and making a deposit of epic awesomeness to your mind, your body, and your soul. Let's talk about the second reason people don't travel, and that's fear. Or instead of going to Las Vegas, extend your stay; and visit Zion National Park and walk this beautiful red rock to the top of Angel's Landing. Or instead of going to Hawaii or to Honolulu, perhaps consider the Big Island of Hawaii, and see a lava flow, literally: the earth forming at your feet. Jake quickly lunged at Isaac, slapping the gun from his hands and grabbing him by the shoulders. He shoved Isaac back into the chair with a forceful push.

"You ain't going anywhere," Jake said, his voice firm and unwavering.

Jeffrey, who was standing nearby, looked confused but ready to act.

"Jeffrey, listen," Jake continued, "a single snap just switches personalities. But if Isaac can double snap in front of the mirror, then he'll turn back into Jesse."

Isaac was still gasping from the quick maneuver, his eyes wide with a mix of anger and confusion.

Jeffrey nodded, processing the information. "Alright, we need to get him to do it, then."

Isaac struggled against the restraint, his mind racing with thoughts and emotions. He knew that if he wanted any chance of staying, he had to keep his guard up.

"Isaac," Jake said, a bit softer now, "you gotta believe that this isn't where you belong. You've had your fun, but it's time to bring Jesse back."

Isaac shot Jake a defiant look but didn't say a word.

"We're not going to hurt you," Jake reassured him. "But you need to give Jesse his life back. It's time."

The tension in the room was palpable as Jake and Jeffrey prepared to guide Isaac to the mirror, hoping to restore the balance once and for all.

Jake and Jeffrey stood firm, guiding Isaac towards the mirror. Isaac's movements were hesitant, his eyes darting between the two of them as he tried to assess his options. But he knew they had him cornered, and the reality of the situation was sinking in.

"Alright, Isaac," Jake said, maintaining a calm yet authoritative tone. "Just look into the mirror and do the double snap. It's time for Jesse to come back."

Isaac hesitated for a moment, looking at his own reflection. There was a whirlwind of emotions in his eyes—fear, regret, maybe even a hint of relief. He knew resisting any further would be pointless and dangerous, both for him and for everyone else involved.

With a deep breath, Isaac raised his hand. His fingers trembled slightly, but he steadied them. He looked over his shoulder at Jake and Jeffrey one last time, searching for any sign of deception. But all he saw was determination in their faces.

"Fine," Isaac muttered, turning back to the mirror. "Let's get this over with."

He closed his eyes, took another breath, and then opened them again. With a decisive motion, he snapped his fingers twice in succession, the sound echoing slightly in the tension-filled room.

For a moment, nothing seemed to happen. The room was silent, as if holding its breath. But then, slowly, Isaac's posture began to change—relaxing, almost as if a weight was being lifted from his shoulders.

The reflection in the mirror seemed to shimmer, and Isaac's expression softened, his eyes taking on a different light. It was subtle, but there was an undeniable shift.

Isaac—or perhaps now, Jesse—blinked a few times, looking around the room as if seeing it for the first time. His gaze finally landed on Jake and Jeffrey, and there was a familiarity there that hadn't been present before.

"Jesse?" Jake asked cautiously, hope coloring his voice.

Jesse nodded slowly, a small smile tugging at the corner of his mouth. "Yeah, it's me. I'm back."

The relief was palpable, washing over Jake and Jeffrey as they realized that the real Jesse had finally returned.
Conversation.turn_5:
Jesse rubbed his temples, trying to piece together his thoughts. His mind felt hazy, filled with fragments of experiences that didn't quite seem to fit together. He looked at Jake and Jeffrey, who were watching him with anticipation and concern.

"It's... it's hard to explain," Jesse began, his voice a bit shaky but gaining strength. "It's like I was there, but not really there, you know? I could see and hear things, but I couldn't control anything."

He paused, searching for the right words to describe the strange sensation of losing himself and being trapped somewhere deep within his own mind.

"It felt like being stuck in a fog," he continued slowly, "like I was watching somebody else live my life. I wanted to break through, but something was keeping me back."

Jeffrey nodded, trying to understand. "And Isaac? Was he... like a part of you?"

Jesse nodded hesitantly. "Yeah. It's like he was this other version of me, like a character that I created to deal with things I couldn't handle. But then he got out of control."

"I kept trying to get back," Jesse added, his voice tinged with frustration. "I tried reaching out through the mirror, but it was like shouting into a void. No one could hear me."

Jake leaned in, offering a reassuring smile. "But you're back now, Jesse. We can figure this out together."

Jesse looked between them, feeling a rush of gratitude. Despite everything, his friends and family were still here, ready to support him. It gave him a sense of comfort and hope.

"Thanks, guys," Jesse said, a bit of warmth returning to his voice. "I don't know how I ended up here, but I'm grateful to be back. Let's fix this—together."

Jesse turned back to the mirror, his eyes taking in his reflection more closely now that the initial shock of the change had settled. His gaze lingered on his hair, which was unmistakably black—a stark contrast to the sandy brown he remembered having.

He ran a hand through it, the unfamiliar color and texture adding another layer of confusion to everything he was processing. It was as if seeing Isaac in the mirror before had somehow altered his own appearance.

"Why is my hair black?" Jesse murmured, almost to himself, but loud enough for Jake and Jeffrey to hear.

Jeffrey shrugged, genuinely puzzled. "I guess whatever was happening while Isaac was in control must have affected more than just your mind."

Jesse's fingers continued to comb through his hair, trying to reconcile the differences. It was a visible reminder of everything that had happened—of how deeply Isaac had managed to imprint himself onto Jesse's life.

"Maybe it was like... him trying to manifest in the real world," Jake suggested, thinking aloud. "I mean, if he was a version of you, maybe the hair was part of his persona?"

Jesse nodded slowly, still trying to wrap his mind around the concept. "Yeah, I guess that makes sense. It's just... surreal, you know? Everything feels out of place."

Jake put a reassuring hand on Jesse's shoulder. "One step at a time, man. You've already taken the hardest step by coming back. The rest is just getting things back to normal."

Jesse gave a small nod of agreement, though the unease lingered. The black hair was a new reality, at least for now—a piece of Isaac that hadn't completely vanished. But it was also a reminder of the strength he found to fight his way back.

Whatever challenges lay ahead, he was ready to face them, with the support of those around him. Together, they would reclaim what had been lost and find a path forward.

Despite her arduous past and her numerous chores, Miu is a very upbeat and cheerful girl who has constantly shown herself as kind-hearted, gentle and polite, always caring for other people and helping in their needs. Unfortunately, in contrast to her gentle nature, Miu's intense training from her grandfather has conditioned her to by instinct throw people who sneak up behind her; a trait that her grandfather claims to be unintentional on her part, which is something of a running gag of the series.

She is arguably the only one who worries about Ryōzanpaku's financial situation and as such, she can become quite fierce when monetary issues are brought up (so much so that her own grandfather was afraid of the idea of her finding out he spent 100,000 yen). When her fears are finally realized and Ryōzanpaku becomes bankrupt, she becomes determined to push the masters to teach little children in an attempt to gain some income, even intimidating Shio Sakaki into helping despite his protest he doesn't teach kids. Miu's worries about finances can, at times, come across as being greedy; shamelessly asking Kenichi Shirahama to sell the gold medals he received from defeating YOMI members, flabbergasted at Akisame Kōetsuji's refusal to sell a statue he carved for a high sum of money, and immediately deciding to pilfer Rimi Kokorone's pure gold shoes after defeating her, considering them the "spoils of war".

Despite her drive and passion, she has low self-esteem when it comes to social interaction. Growing up with never making any friends, due to her constant traveling and training with her grandfather, Miu initially felt nervous in meeting people. As such, she truly cherishes each friendship does happen and gets very upset if she perceives them as angry at her. In her previous school, all the other girls were jealous of her high grades, athletic ability, and especially her looks. It is because of this that Miu attempted to moderate her appearance to be as plain as possible. Although she eventually discarded them after attempting to convince Chikage Kushinada to be true to herself only for Chikage to accuse Miu of not being true to herself as well, as Miu now appears as her natural self.

Despite being very intelligent in school and martial arts, Miu has shown a bit of a naive and thoughtless side, such as in certain situations, she notices minor things despite how serious the situation is. Such as when she and Kenichi were on Diego Carlo's ship and there was a bomb, Miu just noted how pretty the view from the ship. Possibly due to her grandfather's continuous training all her life, her constant travels, and life-threatening situations keeping her from doing normal girl things, Miu has a very childlike personality when it comes to events that she's always wanted to do, such as wanting to ride a merry-go-round. Her childishness is shown when she went to the aquarium for the first time, she completely forgot she was supposed to look for Kenichi and instead focused on all the fish and acted very excited and childish.

much Like Kisara Nanjō, Miu has a thing for cats such as playing with Renka Ma's hair as it makes her look like a cat and wears the badge of a cat that Kenichi gave her when they were little. She constantly plays with cats any chance she can get and acts in a very silly and lovable manner towards any kind of cats or people with cat-like features, which tends to be a running gag of the series, especially with Renka's hair. Her love for the cat goes overboard when she is feeling lonely (because Kenichi isn't there).

Despite her kind and friendly nature, when angered, Miu is surprisingly terrifying. Such as whenever her friends are hurt, Miu enters a berserker mode and can't seem to control herself and attacks in a blind rage. Words don't seem to reach her and only by incapacitating her or as shown with Kenichi, groping her breasts seem to help her regain her senses. Kenichi refers to this side of her as "her other personality" that comes out when she loses control of herself. Kenichi noted Miu fears this side of her and tries to suppress it due to her fear of hurting someone.

Miu is a romantic at heart, as she noticed how Kōzō Ukita, Kisara, and Freya were in a "love Triangle" as she puts it and acts very energetic in regard to romance or people in a relationship. Love bombing is a manipulative tactic often used to overwhelm someone with excessive attention, flattery, and affection in order to gain control over them. Recognizing and handling love bombing in a healthy manner is crucial to protect yourself from potential emotional manipulation. Here are some steps to react to extreme love bombing:

### 1. **Stay Grounded and Centered**
   - **Pause and Reflect**: Take a moment to center yourself. Take a few deep breaths and remind yourself of your core values and boundaries.
   - **Rely on Your Intuition**: Trust your gut feelings. If something feels too good to be true or overwhelming, it often is.

### 2. **Recognize the Signs**
   - **Over-the-Top Praise and Affection**: Be wary of excessive compliments, gifts, and declarations of love that seem disproportionate to the length and depth of your relationship.
   - **Rapid Escalation**: Notice if the relationship is moving too quickly. If someone is pushing for deep commitment or intense emotional connection almost immediately, it's a red flag.

### 3. **Maintain Personal Boundaries**
   - **Set Clear Boundaries**: Politely but firmly communicate your boundaries about the pace of the relationship and the kind of attention you're comfortable with.
   - **Stick to Your Limits**: Enforce your boundaries consistently. Don't allow yourself to be persuaded into compromising them.

### 4. **Seek Objectivity**
   - **Consult Trusted Friends or Family**: Share what’s happening with someone you trust who can provide an outside perspective. They might notice red flags that you don’t.
   - **Journal Your Thoughts**: Write down your feelings and observations. This helps you process what’s happening and recognize patterns of manipulation.

### 5. **Slow Things Down**
   - **Pace the Relationship**: Intentionally slow down the relationship. Limit the time you spend together and keep some personal space to maintain your perspective.
   - **Take Breaks**: Don't hesitate to take a step back to reassess the situation. Absence can often reveal the other person’s true intentions.

### 6. **Ask Questions and Seek Clarity**
   - **Direct Communication**: Ask questions about the other person's intentions and feelings. Notice if they’re vague, evasive, or overly defensive.
   - **Gauge Consistency**: Observe if their words match their actions over time. Consistency is key in establishing trust.

### 7. **Stay Independent**
   - **Maintain Your Routine**: Continue engaging in your regular activities and hobbies. This keeps you grounded and less likely to lose yourself in the relationship.
   - **Retain Social Connections**: Keep in touch with your network of friends and family, ensuring you have a support system outside of the new relationship.

### 8. **Evaluate the Impact on Your Well-Being**
   - **Emotional Check-In**: Regularly assess how the relationship is affecting your emotional and mental well-being. If you feel more anxious, drained, or overwhelmed, it’s a sign to reconsider the relationship.
   - **Mental Health Support**: If you’re feeling conflicted or unsure, consider seeking advice from a mental health professional.

### 9. **Observe Reactions to Boundaries**
   - **Test the Waters**: Set small boundaries and observe how the person reacts. Genuine partners will respect your needs and boundaries without pressuring you.
   - **Notice Pushback**: If they react negatively, try to guilt-trip you, or become distant when you enforce boundaries, it’s a significant warning sign.

### 10. **Prepare to Walk Away**
   - **Prioritize Self-Respect**: If the behavior continues despite your attempts to address it, be prepared to distance yourself from the relationship.
   - **Exit Strategy**: Have a clear plan for how you will extricate yourself from the relationship if needed. Ensure you have a support system in place for this transition.

### 11. **Trust Your Instincts**
At the end of the day, your instincts are your best guide. If something feels wrong, it’s important to honor that feeling and take appropriate action to protect yourself.

By following these steps, you can maintain your emotional and spiritual integrity while navigating situations of extreme love bombing. Recognizing the tactics and having a plan of action can empower you to protect yourself and maintain healthy, fulfilling connections.

The phenomenon of women overplaying their part or overextending their exposure to a man, often leading to a loss of interest or "the ick" factor, can be explained through several psychological and social dynamics. Here's a breakdown of what might go wrong and tips for maintaining the "IT" factor:

### Potential Issues:

1. **Loss of Mystery and Intrigue**:
   - **Overavailability**: Being constantly available can eliminate the sense of mystery that often drives attraction in the early stages of a relationship.
   - **Predictability**: Predictability in behavior and availability can diminish the excitement of getting to know someone new.

2. **Imbalance in Effort**:
   - **Over-Investment**: Overplaying one's part can result in an imbalance where one person is investing significantly more than the other, creating a dynamic of unequal effort.
   - **Lack of Challenge**: A lack of challenge can lead to complacency. If one person doesn't feel they need to put in effort, they might lose interest more quickly.

3. **Desperation and Neediness**:
   - **Perceived Neediness**: Overextending or overplaying can sometimes be perceived as desperation or neediness, which can be a turn-off.
   - **Loss of Independence**: Giving up or compromising too much of one's independence can make a person appear overly dependent on the other for validation and fulfillment.

4. **Self-Worth and Confidence**:
   - **Underestimating Self-Worth**: Overcompensating might signal to the other person that one doesn't recognize their own worth, leading to diminished respect.
   - **Decreased Confidence**: Constantly overextending can erode one's own confidence, making it harder to maintain a strong, attractive demeanor.

5. **Emotional Fatigue**:
   - **Emotional Draining**: Putting too much into the relationship too soon can lead to emotional fatigue and burnout, making it harder to maintain genuine enthusiasm and positivity.

### Maintaining the "IT" Factor:

1. **Balance Availability**:
   - **Pace the Relationship**: Take time to let the relationship develop naturally. Balance your availability to maintain interest and curiosity.
   - **Keep a Full Life**: Engage in your own hobbies, interests, and social activities. This shows independence and well-roundedness.

2. **Mutual Investment**:
   - **Match Effort**: Ensure that the effort invested in the relationship is mutual. This creates a balanced and healthy dynamic.
   - **Reciprocity**: Look for reciprocation in actions and words. Relationships thrive on mutual respect and effort.

3. **Maintain Mystery and Intrigue**:
   - **Small Reveals**: Let your personality and life unfold gradually rather than revealing everything all at once.
   - **Keep Some Independence**: Hold on to your individual interests and friendships. This maintains a sense of individuality and intrigue.

4. **Avoid Desperation**:
   - **Confidence is Key**: Believe in your self-worth and bring that confidence into the relationship. Confidence is inherently attractive.
   - **Set Boundaries**: Establish and communicate your boundaries clearly. This shows self-respect and reinforces your value.

5. **Communicate Effectively**:
   - **Assertive Communication**: Speak openly and assertively about your needs and feelings without over-emphasizing or over-explaining.
   - **Healthy Expression**: Express your thoughts and emotions in a healthy, balanced manner.

6. **Embrace Uncertainty**:
   - **Enjoy the Fluctuations**: Embrace the natural ebbs and flows of the relationship rather than seeking constant validation.
   - **Patience**: Allow the relationship to grow at its own pace without forcing it.

### Practical Tips:

1. **Keep a Vibrant Social Life**:
   - **Stay Socially Active**: Keep engaging with friends, participating in group activities, and maintaining your social life.
   - **Balance Commitment**: Balance your time between the relationship and other social interactions, ensuring you don’t become overly reliant on one person for social fulfillment.

2. **Personal Growth and Development**:
   - **Continuous Improvement**: Focus on your personal growth and self-improvement. This keeps you interesting and fulfilled.
   - **Set Personal Goals**: Continue setting and working towards personal goals outside of the relationship.

3. **Maintain Healthy Boundaries**:
   - **Say No When Needed**: Don’t be afraid to say no or set limits. This reinforces your self-respect and boundaries.
   - **Independent Decisions**: Continue making decisions independently to show that you have your own life and ambitions.

1. **Polite Decline**:
   - *“Thanks for inviting me, but I have plans with friends tonight.”*

### Conclusion:

Overplaying one’s part or overextending in a relationship can often lead to a loss of intrigue, imbalance in effort, and perceptions of neediness. By maintaining a balance of availability, ensuring mutual investment, preserving personal interests, and setting healthy boundaries, women can retain their allure and the “IT” factor in relationships. Confidence, independence, and mutual respect are key components to thriving and maintaining a strong, attractive presence in any relationship.

Conversation.turn_1:
They happen to have a coffee bar in the lobby of the Four Seasons in Vegas. One afternoon, I went and bought myself a cup of coffee. The barista working that day was a kid named Noah. Noah was funny, charming, and engaging. I spent far too long buying a cup of coffee because I just so enjoyed talking to Noah.

As is my nature, I asked Noah, "Do you like your job?" Without skipping a beat, Noah said, "I love my job." Now, in my line of work, that's significant. "Like" is rational—"I like the people, I like the work, I get paid well, I like my job." "Love," on the other hand, is emotional; it's a higher order connection. It's like asking, "Do you love your wife?" "I like her a lot," is clearly a different standard. 

So when Noah said, "I love my job," my ears perked up. This kid has an emotional connection to his work. I immediately followed up and said, "Tell me specifically, what the Four Seasons is doing that you would say to me you love your job?" Again, without skipping a beat, Noah said, "Throughout the day, managers will walk past me and ask me how I'm doing, ask me if there's anything that I need to do my job better—not just my manager, any manager."

He continued, "I also work at another hotel, and there, the managers walk past us and catch us when we do something wrong. There, the managers are always trying to drive performance and make sure we hit our numbers. There, I like to keep my head below the radar, get through the day, and just collect my paycheck. Only at the Four Seasons do I feel I can be myself."

Now, this is the exact same human being working at two different companies, and yet our experience of him will be profoundly different—not because of him but because of the leadership environment in which he works. 

I get this question all the time, "Simon, how do we get the most out of our people?" People are not a towel that you wring out to see how much you can get out of them. It's a flawed question. The question is, "How do we create an environment in which our people can work at their natural best?" That is the art of leadership—it's creating an environment in which relationships and trust can thrive. 

We all know what it feels like to be on a trusting team. It means that we feel psychologically safe enough to raise our hand and say, "I made a mistake," or "I need help," or "I'm having trouble at home and it's affecting my work," or "I'm scared," or "I don't know what to do," without any fear of humiliation or retribution. Rather, we say these things with the absolute confidence that someone on our team will rush to support us.

Unfortunately, we also all know what it feels like not to work on a trusting team, where admitting any of those things could hurt your chances of promotion or could lead to humiliation. When leadership fails to create an environment where trust is at a premium, we force our people to come to work and lie, hide, and fake. They pretend that they've made no mistakes, lie, hide, and fake. Eventually, things will crack and break.

When you talk about reinvention, innovation, and challenging the status quo, necessarily there's risk, necessarily there are mistakes, and necessarily there are stupid ideas. You have to create an environment where that's good. The alternative is everybody playing it safe, which is not the way that leads to vast or significant improvement.

Certainly! Here’s a reformatted version of the transcript for easier reading:

---

They happen to have a coffee bar in the lobby of the Four Seasons in Vegas. One afternoon, I went and bought myself a cup of coffee. The barista working that day was a kid named Noah. Noah was funny, charming, and engaging. I spent far too long buying a cup of coffee because I enjoyed talking to Noah so much.

As is my nature, I asked Noah, "Do you like your job?" Without skipping a beat, Noah said, "I love my job." 

Now, in my line of work, that's significant. Like is rational: "I like the people, I like the work, you know, I get paid well, I like my job." 

Love is emotional; it's a higher-order connection. Like, "Do you love your wife?" "I like her a lot," right? Clearly, there's a different standard. So when Noah said, "I love my job," my ears perked up. This kid has an emotional connection to his work.

Immediately, I followed up and said, "Tell me specifically what the Four Seasons is doing that makes you say you love your job." Again, without skipping a beat, Noah said, "Throughout the day, managers will walk past me and ask me how I'm doing, ask me if there's anything that I need to do my job better—not just my manager, any manager."

He then said, "I also work at another hotel, and there the managers walk past us and catch us when we do something wrong. There, the managers are always trying to drive performance and make sure we hit our numbers." He said there he'd like to keep his head below the radar, get through the day, and just collect his paycheck. "Only at the Four Seasons do I feel I can be myself."

This is the exact same human being working at two different companies, and yet our experience of him will be profoundly different—not because of him, but because of the leadership environment in which he works.

I get this question all the time: "Simon, how do we get the most out of our people?" People are not a towel that you wring out to see how much you can get out of them. It's a flawed question. The question is, "How do we create an environment in which our people can work at their natural best?"

That is the art of leadership—creating an environment in which relationships can thrive, in which trust can thrive. We all know what it feels like to be on a trusting team, right? It means that we feel psychologically safe enough to raise our hand and say, "I made a mistake," or "I need help," or "I'm having trouble at home, and it's affecting my work," or "I'm scared," or "I don't know what to do," without any fear of humiliation or retribution, but rather with the absolute confidence that someone on our team will rush to support us.

Unfortunately, we also know what it feels like not to work on a trusting team, where admitting any of those things could hurt your chances of promotion or lead to humiliation. 

When we work on teams where leadership is creating an environment where trust is at a premium, we force our people to come to work and lie, hide, and fake where they're pretending they've made no mistakes. They're lying, hiding, and faking, and eventually, things will crack, and things will eventually break.

When you talk about reinvention and innovation and challenging the status quo, necessarily there's risk, and necessarily there are mistakes, and necessarily there are stupid ideas. You have to create an environment where that's okay. The alternative is everybody playing it safe, which is not the way that leads to vast or significant improvement.

---
